b: Bishop of Grenoble for fifty-two years, who gave Bruno and his six companions the mountain valley of the Chartreuse in 1084 and thereby founded the Carthusians. He begged to resign to become a monk himself; three popes refused.

A Calabrian hermit whose followers, the Minims ('the least'), took a fourth vow of perpetual Lent. Summoned to France to cure Louis XI, he instead prepared the king to die. Legend has him crossing the Strait of Messina on his cloak. Patron of sailors.

An Oxford scholar who ploughed his family's fields to save them from ruin, became chancellor of the university and bishop of Chichester against King Henry III's will, and lived like a poor priest. His prayer 'Day by day, dear Lord, of thee three things I pray' is still sung.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Archbishop of Seville who converted the Visigothic kings from Arianism, presided over the councils of Toledo, and wrote the Etymologies — an encyclopaedia of all ancient knowledge that was the most-copied book of the early Middle Ages. Proposed as patron of the internet.

A Valencian Dominican who preached the end of the world across Spain, France and Italy for twenty years, followed by crowds of penitents, and worked to end the Great Schism though he had served the Avignon pope. Patron of builders.

A Paris canon called to Denmark to reform a lax monastery, who persevered through poverty and hostility to found Æbelholt abbey. Also today: Notker the Stammerer of St Gall, poet of the sequences, whose hymns are still sung at Mass.

t: Priest, founder of the Christian Brothers
b: A canon of Reims who gave his fortune to the poor and founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools — teaching in French instead of Latin, in classes instead of one by one, with training colleges for teachers. Patron of teachers.

A Picardy peasant paralysed for twenty-two years, who from her bed taught catechism and hid priests during the Terror, was suddenly healed, and founded the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur to teach poor girls. 'How good is the good God!'

A Belgian noblewoman whose parents, husband, sister and four children are all saints; when her husband became a monk she founded the convent around which the city of Mons grew. Also today: Casilda of Toledo, the Moorish princess who fed Christian prisoners.

Bishop and founder of the cathedral school of Chartres, the first great school of the eleventh century; he rebuilt the cathedral after the fire of 1020 and wrote the Easter hymn Chorus novae Jerusalem.

Bishop of Kraków who excommunicated King Boleslaus II for his cruelties and was cut down by the king himself at the altar of St Michael's church. Poland's Thomas Becket; Kraków's cathedral holds his relics beside the Polish kings.

An African-born bishop of Verona whose ninety surviving sermons show a Church fresh from persecution: he baptised the crowd every Easter, insisted that the wealthy share, and is shown with a fish on his crozier. Also today: Julius I, the pope who defended Athanasius.

The last pope venerated as a martyr. Elected without the emperor's consent, he condemned Monothelitism at the Lateran Council; Constans II had him kidnapped, tried in Constantinople, stripped, chained and exiled to the Crimea, where he died of hunger and neglect.

Valerian, the husband of Cecilia, converted by her on their wedding night; Tiburtius his brother; and Maximus the officer who was to execute them and instead joined them. They were buried by Cecilia on the Appian Way.

A noblewoman of Alsace who washed the clothes of the poor of her village with her own hands. Also today: Damien of Molokai (traditional date), the Belgian priest who lived and died among the lepers of Hawaii — 'We lepers.'

The visionary of Lourdes died on this day in 1879 (see February 18). Also today: Benedict Joseph Labre, the French beggar who wandered Europe's shrines in rags for thirteen years, sleeping in the ruins of the Colosseum, and died in Holy Week to the cry of the children of Rome, 'The saint is dead!'

An Englishman who became the third abbot of Cîteaux and saved the dying reform by receiving the young Bernard and his thirty companions in 1112. His Charter of Charity gave the Cistercians their constitution; the Cîteaux Bible he corrected against the Hebrew survives.

A Roman senator denounced as a Christian by his own slave under Commodus; his defence before the Senate, one of the earliest Christian apologies, is preserved. He was beheaded. Also today: Galdinus of Milan, who died in the pulpit preaching against heresy.

An Alsatian bishop who entered Rome barefoot as a pilgrim to be elected, and travelled Europe holding councils against simony and clerical marriage with Hildebrand and Humbert at his side. He died months before his legate's excommunication of the patriarch of Constantinople began the Great Schism.

Made prioress at fifteen by papal dispensation, she founded a Dominican convent in her home town and lived on bread and water. Catherine of Siena visited her incorrupt body and, bending to kiss the foot, saw it lift to meet her.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Abbot of Bec and archbishop of Canterbury, exiled twice by Norman kings over the freedom of the Church. His Proslogion offers the ontological argument — God as 'that than which nothing greater can be thought' — and Cur Deus Homo asks why God became man. 'Faith seeking understanding.'

Soter (d. 174) was praised by Dionysius of Corinth for the alms Rome sent to poor churches; Caius (d. 296), a Dalmatian, ruled through the calm before Diocletian's storm. Also today: Theodore of Sykeon, the innkeeper's son who became a bishop and a wonder-worker.

A soldier of Cappadocia martyred at Lydda under Diocletian; the dragon came later, from the Golden Legend. Crusaders brought him to England, where he displaced Edward the Confessor as patron. Also today: Adalbert of Prague, apostle of the Prussians, martyred in 997.

A lawyer known as 'the poor man's advocate' who became a Capuchin and was sent to preach to the Calvinists of the Grisons; he was cut down by a mob at Seewis after preaching on 'one Lord, one faith, one baptism'. First martyr of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith.

John Mark of Jerusalem, in whose mother's house the Church met, who turned back on Paul's first journey and later became 'my son' to Peter, whose preaching he set down in the shortest and earliest Gospel. Founder of the Church of Alexandria; his relics were smuggled to Venice in 828 under a load of pork.

A fresco of the Virgin and Child that, tradition says, appeared on a wall at Genazzano near Rome in 1467; the sanctuary became a place of pilgrimage for popes. Also today: Cletus and Marcellinus, early popes.

A servant in the Fatinelli household at Lucca for forty-eight years, who gave her food to the poor and once, legend says, had her baking done by angels while she prayed. Patroness of domestic workers; her body lies incorrupt in San Frediano.

A Marist missionary to the island of Futuna in the Pacific, clubbed to death by the king's warriors when the king's son asked for baptism. Within a year the whole island was Christian. First martyr of Oceania. Also today: Louis de Montfort, apostle of Marian consecration.

t: Virgin and Doctor of the Church, patroness of Europe
b: The twenty-fourth child of a Sienese dyer, a Dominican tertiary who nursed plague victims, dictated the Dialogue in ecstasy, told the pope to his face to return from Avignon to Rome — and he did. She died at thirty-three. The first woman named Doctor of the Church, with Teresa of Ávila.

A Dominican inquisitor who as pope enforced the reforms of Trent, published the Roman Catechism, Breviary and Missal, and organised the Holy League that won at Lepanto — he is said to have known of the victory by vision before the news arrived. He still wore his white Dominican habit; popes have worn white since.

Instituted by Pius XII in 1955 to set the carpenter of Nazareth beside the workers' May Day: the dignity of labour in the hands that taught the Son of God to use a plane. Also today: Peregrine Laziosi, patron of cancer patients, and the prophet Jeremias in the Martyrology.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Bishop of Alexandria for forty-five years, seventeen of them in five exiles, for insisting against the Arian emperors that the Son is 'of one substance with the Father'. Athanasius contra mundum — 'against the world'. He wrote the Life of Anthony and first listed exactly our twenty-seven New Testament books.

Philip of Bethsaida, who brought Nathanael to Jesus and asked at the Last Supper, 'Lord, show us the Father'; and James the Less, son of Alphaeus. Their relics lie together in the church of the Twelve Apostles in Rome, dedicated on this day.

A Roman officer in Noricum who declared himself a Christian when ordered to persecute them, and was drowned in the Enns with a millstone round his neck. Patron of Austria, Poland and firefighters. Also today: the English Martyrs of the Reformation (England and Wales).

A monk of Lérins made archbishop of Arles at twenty-nine, who worked with his hands to feed the poor and sold the church plate to ransom captives. His quarrel with Pope Leo the Great over the limits of his authority is a landmark in the history of the papacy.

A boy of the oratory at Turin who resolved at his First Communion, 'Death rather than sin', broke up fights with a crucifix, and died at fourteen. Don Bosco wrote his life; Pius XII canonised him in 1954 as the youngest non-martyr saint of his time.

Bishop of Hexham and York who ordained the Venerable Bede, and retired to the monastery he founded at Beverley. Henry V attributed Agincourt, fought on the day of his translation, to his prayers. Also today: Rose Venerini, foundress of the first public schools for girls in Italy.

The archangel's appearance on Monte Gargano in Apulia in 492, where a cave became the oldest Michael shrine in the West; pilgrims and crusaders have climbed to it ever since. Also today: Peter of Tarentaise, the Cistercian archbishop who fled his see to hide as a lay brother.

A pagan conscript in the Egyptian army converted by the kindness of Christians to the prisoners, who founded at Tabennisi the first monastery where monks lived under a common rule — nine monasteries and three thousand monks by his death. Basil and Benedict both built on his rule.

A Flemish farmer's son who volunteered for the leper colony of Kalaupapa on Molokai, built its church, coffins and homes with his own hands, and after sixteen years began a sermon 'We lepers'. He died of the disease at forty-nine. Patron of those with leprosy and HIV. Also today: John of Ávila, Doctor of the Church.

A Sardinian peasant who for forty years begged for his friary through the streets of Cagliari, refusing the alms of a usurer, and was loved by the whole city. Also today: Mamertus of Vienne, who instituted the Rogation days of prayer for the harvest.

Nereus and Achilleus, Praetorian soldiers who threw away their arms, and Pancras, a fourteen-year-old Phrygian orphan beheaded under Diocletian. Augustine of Canterbury dedicated his first church in England to Pancras; the London station keeps the name.

On 13 May 1917 three shepherd children — Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta — saw a lady 'brighter than the sun' over a holm oak at the Cova da Iria in Portugal, who asked for the Rosary and returned on the thirteenth of each month until October, when seventy thousand saw the sun dance. John Paul II was shot on this day in 1981 and credited her with his life.

After the Ascension the Eleven chose by lot, between Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias, one 'who accompanied us all the time the Lord Jesus came in and went out among us' to take Judas's place. Nothing more is known; tradition sends him to Ethiopia.

A day labourer of Madrid who went to Mass before work every morning; his employer, checking why he was late to the fields, found angels ploughing beside him. He and his wife Maria de la Cabeza shared their food with the poor and the birds. Patron of Madrid and of farmers.

An English Carmelite general to whom, tradition says, the Virgin gave the brown scapular in 1251 at Cambridge. He steered the order from Palestinian hermits to European friars. Also today: Brendan the Navigator, whose legendary voyage may have touched America, and John Nepomucene, drowned in the Vltava.

A Spanish shepherd who taught himself to read to pray the office, became a Franciscan doorkeeper, and adored the Blessed Sacrament for hours at night. Patron of Eucharistic congresses; his tomb at Villareal was desecrated in 1936.

Sent by the Arian king Theodoric to Constantinople to plead for the Arians of the East — the first pope to visit the city — he was received with such honour that Theodoric, suspecting treachery, imprisoned him at Ravenna on his return, where he died of ill-treatment.

Abbot of Glastonbury, adviser to seven kings, and archbishop who restored English monasticism after the Danes. A skilled metalworker and harpist — legend says he seized the devil's nose with his tongs. Also today: Celestine V, the hermit pope who resigned, and Ivo of Kermartin, patron of lawyers.

The greatest preacher of fifteenth-century Italy, who held crowds for hours in the piazzas, ended feuds, burned vanities, and held up the monogram IHS of the Holy Name until it was painted on every city gate. He refused three bishoprics.

Twenty-two priests and three laymen shot during the Cristero War, when the Mexican government closed the churches. Magallanes, a parish priest who had founded a seminary, gave his executioners absolution and his remaining possessions: 'I die innocent, and I ask God that my blood may serve to unite my Mexican brethren.'

Married at twelve to a violent man she reformed by patience, widowed when he was murdered, and bereft of two sons who died before they could avenge him; then an Augustinian nun who bore a thorn-wound from a crucifix for fifteen years. Patroness of impossible causes.

A Roman priest, epileptic, who spent his life among the cattle-drovers of the Campagna, the beggars and the homeless women of Rome, hearing confessions all day. He gave away everything and died in a hospital bed. Also today: Desiderius of Vienne, martyred by Queen Brunhilda.

Instituted by Pius VII in 1815 in thanks for his release from Napoleon's prison; the title comes from the Litany of Loreto after Lepanto. Don Bosco built the great basilica of Turin under it. Also today: David of Scotland, the king who founded Melrose and Holyrood.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: A monk of Jarrow from the age of seven who never travelled beyond Northumbria and wrote the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, the first history of England and the book that popularised dating years from Christ's birth. He died dictating a translation of John's Gospel: 'It is finished.' Also today: Gregory VII and Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi.

The 'Apostle of Rome', a Florentine layman who spent seventeen years praying in the catacombs and talking to anyone, then founded the Oratory where laymen prayed, sang and laughed together; his heart was physically enlarged by a vision at Pentecost. 'Be good, if you can.'

Prior of Gregory the Great's monastery in Rome, sent with forty monks to Kent in 597, so afraid of the English that he turned back once. King Ethelbert met him under an oak, was baptised, and gave him Canterbury. Gregory's letters answering his practical questions are in Bede.

Archdeacon of Aosta who built hospices on the two Alpine passes that bear his name, staffed by canons and their dogs, to rescue pilgrims to Rome from the snow. Patron of mountaineers. Also today: Germanus of Paris, whose abbey became Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

Giovanni Battista Montini, who completed the Second Vatican Council, reformed the liturgy and the calendar, was the first pope to fly, to visit the Holy Land and to address the United Nations, and wrote Humanae Vitae. Also today: Maximinus of Trier, who sheltered Athanasius in exile.

A peasant girl of Domrémy whose voices sent her at seventeen to raise the siege of Orléans and crown Charles VII at Reims; captured by the Burgundians, sold to the English, condemned by a church court and burned at Rouen at nineteen. Her sentence was annulled in 1456 and she was canonised in 1920.

n: The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: Mary hurries to the hill country to her cousin Elizabeth, and John leaps in the womb at her greeting: 'Blessed art thou among women.' Her answer is the Magnificat, sung by the Church every evening since. The feast closes the month of Mary.

A Samaritan philosopher who tried the Stoics, Aristotelians and Pythagoreans before an old man on a beach pointed him to the prophets. He kept his philosopher's cloak, opened a school in Rome, wrote the Apologies describing the Sunday Eucharist to the emperor, and was beheaded with six students.

A priest and an exorcist beheaded in a wood outside Rome under Diocletian so that their graves would not be found; their executioner told the story after becoming a Christian. Constantine built a basilica over them and buried his mother beside it. Named in the Roman Canon.

Twenty-two pages of the court of King Mwanga of Buganda, Catholics and Anglicans, aged thirteen to thirty, who refused the king's demands and were burned alive at Namugongo. Charles, master of the pages, had baptised four of them the night before. Africa's first canonised martyrs.

A Neapolitan noble cured of leprosy who founded the Clerks Regular Minor, vowed not to seek office, and spent nights in adoration: 'Zeal for thy house has eaten me up' was found written over his heart. Also today: Optatus of Milevis, who answered the Donatists.

t: Bishop and martyr, apostle of Germany
b: Winfrid of Devon, who felled the sacred oak of Thor at Geismar before a crowd waiting for the god to strike him, founded Fulda, crowned Pepin, and reformed the Frankish Church. At seventy-nine he went back to the Frisians and was killed at Dokkum, holding a Gospel book over his head.

A worldly courtier thrown from his horse by lightning, who became a wandering preacher, founded the white canons at Prémontré, and as archbishop of Magdeburg fought for the reform of the clergy. Patron of Bohemia; his relics are at Strahov in Prague.

One of the founders of Fountains Abbey and first abbot of Newminster in Northumberland; the hermit Godric saw his soul rise to heaven as a ball of fire. Also today: Colman of Dromore and Meriadoc of Vannes.

Twice archbishop of York, deposed through the intrigues of the Cistercians and restored after Bernard's death; as he re-entered York the Ouse bridge collapsed under the crowd and no one was hurt. He died a month later, perhaps poisoned in the chalice. Also today: Medard, patron of the weather.

t: Deacon and Doctor of the Church
b: 'The harp of the Holy Spirit', a deacon of Nisibis and Edessa who wrote theology as hymns — hundreds of them, sung by choirs of women he trained — and never accepted ordination as a priest. He died nursing the victims of famine. Also today: Columba of Iona.

An English princess raised in Hungary who married Malcolm III of Scotland, reformed the Scottish Church, fed orphans with her own hands every morning, and founded Dunfermline. Her son David is a saint; her chapel is the oldest building in Edinburgh. (November 16 in the new calendar.)

Joseph of Cyprus, 'son of consolation', who sold his field for the apostles, vouched for the converted Saul when everyone feared him, fetched him from Tarsus to Antioch, and shared his first journey — then parted from him over Mark. Tradition says he was stoned at Salamis.

A preacher of Salamanca who reconciled the feuding nobles of the city and was, it is said, poisoned by a woman whose lover he had converted. Also today: Onuphrius, the hairy hermit of the Egyptian desert loved by medieval pilgrims.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: A Portuguese Augustinian who became a Franciscan after seeing the bodies of the first Franciscan martyrs of Morocco, was discovered as a preacher by accident at an ordination, and held Italy and France spellbound; the fish of Rimini listened when the heretics would not. He died at thirty-five. Patron of lost things.

The Roman Martyrology today remembers Eliseus, disciple and successor of Elias, on whom the double portion of his spirit fell. Also today: Methodius of Constantinople, who restored the icons in 843 — the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy'.

A Sicilian boy, his tutor and his nurse, martyred under Diocletian; Vitus became one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, invoked against epilepsy and the dancing mania called St Vitus's dance. Also today: Germaine Cousin, the sickly shepherdess of Pibrac whose apron of bread turned to flowers.

A Jesuit who walked the mountains of the Vivarais in winter preaching to Huguenots and Catholics alike, founded refuges for prostitutes, and died of pneumonia caught on a mission. The Curé of Ars made a pilgrimage to his grave on foot as a seminarian.

A wealthy Pisan musician converted by a hermit, who lived as a beggar in the Holy Land for years and returned to Pisa to a life of prayer and miracles; his tomb is in the cathedral. Also today: Emily de Vialar, foundress of the Sisters of St Joseph of the Apparition.
See June 9. Also today: Mark and Marcellian, twin brothers of Rome martyred under Diocletian, encouraged by Sebastian when their parents begged them to apostatise.

Founder of the Camaldolese (see February 7 in the traditional calendar): a wanderer who founded hermitages across Italy, and wrote for his hermits the Brief Rule — 'Empty yourself completely and sit waiting, content with the grace of God, like the chick who tastes nothing and eats nothing but what his mother brings him.'

Son of Pope Hormisdas, deposed by the general Belisarius at the empress Theodora's command for refusing to restore a Monophysite patriarch, and starved to death on the island of Palmarola. Also today: Alban, the first martyr of Britain (traditional date).

Heir to the marquisate of Castiglione, who renounced it at seventeen to become a Jesuit against his father's fury, and died at twenty-three nursing plague victims in Rome. Patron of youth and of AIDS caregivers.

Fisher, bishop of Rochester, the only English bishop to refuse Henry VIII's supremacy, beheaded on June 22; More, lord chancellor, author of Utopia, beheaded on July 6: 'I die the king's good servant, and God's first.' Also today: Paulinus of Nola, the senator-poet.

A Piedmontese priest, hunchbacked and tireless, who trained the clergy of Turin, was Don Bosco's confessor and benefactor, and accompanied sixty condemned men to the gallows — 'my hanged saints', he called them. Also today: Etheldreda, foundress of Ely.

n: The Nativity of Saint John the Baptist
b: Six months before Christmas, at midsummer, the Church keeps the birthday of the forerunner — the only saint besides the Virgin whose birth is a feast. His father Zachary's tongue is loosed to sing the Benedictus. 'He must increase, but I must decrease': the days shorten from here.

A married layman of Marseilles who defended Augustine's teaching on grace against the monks of Lérins and became secretary to Leo the Great. Also today: William of Vercelli, founder of Montevergine, and Adalbert of Egmond.

Two brothers, officers of the household of Constantine's daughter, martyred in their own house on the Caelian hill under Julian the Apostate; the basilica built over it stands on the excavated rooms. Named in the Roman Canon. Also today: Josemaría Escrivá, founder of Opus Dei.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Patriarch of Alexandria who fought Nestorius for the title Theotokos and presided at the Council of Ephesus (431) which defined that Mary is the Mother of God, since her child is one person, divine and human. A fierce man; a decisive theologian. Also today: Our Lady of Perpetual Help.

t: Bishop and martyr, Doctor of the Church
b: A pupil of Polycarp who was a pupil of John, bishop of Lyon after the martyrs of 177. His Against Heresies demolished the Gnostics with the rule of faith and the succession of bishops; 'the glory of God is a living man.' Named Doctor of the Church in 2022.

wp: Feast of Saints Peter and Paul
b: The two pillars, martyred at Rome under Nero: Peter crucified head-down on the Vatican hill, Paul beheaded on the Ostian Way. Rome keeps their feast as its own birthday; the pallium is given to new archbishops today. 'Thou art Peter'; 'I have fought the good fight.'

n: The First Martyrs of the Church of Rome
wp: First Martyrs of the Church of Rome
b: The Christians Nero blamed for the fire of 64 and killed in his gardens — sewn into animal skins for the dogs, crucified, or burned as torches to light the night, as Tacitus records. Peter and Paul died in the same persecution.
